items.titleEn: Team news: Havertz and Calafiori return against Sunderland
items.summaryEn: Find out Mikel Arteta's starting XI to take on Sunderland
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has made four changes to the side that beat Napoli in midweek as we take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.
After our European exploits on Wednesday night, the manager has reverted to the team that started our last league match, the win over Chelsea last weekend.

That means Riccardo Calafiori comes back into the defence, while Myles Lewis-Skelly is restored in midfield. Christos Tzolis – fresh from his match-winning assist in the Champions League – starts on the left, while Kai Havertz leads the line up front.
The four to drop to the bench are Piero Hincapie, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres.
There is also a place among the subs for Jurrien Timber, back from injury to be included in the squad for the first time this season.
Sunderland beat Hull City 1-0 in midweek in the Carabao Cup, but their line up today is the same that started their last Premier League match, a 1-1 draw at Brentford last weekend.
So former Gunners Granit Xhaka and Dan Ballard – who scored in this fixture last season – both start.

items.titleEn: Horseman calls for ruthlessness after Chelsea loss
items.summaryEn: Our under-21s head coach felt the game got away from us after missed chances
bodyEn: David Horseman felt we didn't do our performance justice against Chelsea on Saturday, as we lost an open game 4-1 at Meadow Park.
Despite having only two shots fewer than our London rivals, we fell to a heavy defeat as the Blues proved more the more clinical of the two sides.
"The game was decided by big moments," Horseman reflected, "I think we had plenty of chances to score.
"We didn't play with enough conviction in the final third, and when we went through one-on-one or could've had a tap-in from five or six yards, we didn't really ram it home where they did.
"I thought that was the biggest difference in the game, and then obviously, once we go behind, you're chasing as you open up against them.
"They were ruthless with the chances they got, and unfortunately, today, we weren't with the ones we got, and it punished us in the end."
While the game didn't go to plan, Horseman felt that, overall, our start to the season has been positive.
In fact, our under-21s head coach saw plenty that he liked from his side on Saturday, especially in the way we created our abundance of chances.
"There were some really good moments today. We're a new, developing group, so we understand we'll get better.
"It hurts today, because we want to beat them and we had enough chances to probably get something out of the game, but we've had a positive start.

"There's loads we've got to get better at, when we get big chances, and we're creating more this year, we have to take them, we've still got to be far more aggressive, if you look at our first team they win so many duels.

"But the score in the end runs away with us, and it looks probably not a fair reflection in the game. Although they did deserve to win, for us to create as much as we did against a team like that, I think that should hold us in good stead for the rest of the season."
One of the challenges Horseman has faced with our under-21s this season has been the wide range of ages in the squad.
From second year scholars to players with Premier League experience, our Premier League 2 group has a bit of everything.
"That's the beauty of being a big club." Horseman said, admitting he enjoys the challenge.
"I was away with the Youth League team until Wednesday, so I haven't seen Jaden [Dixon], [James] Scanlon or Evan [Mooney] all week until yesterday.

"Then obviously half the group were training with the under-19s, and then they come back together. So that's why I think we'll get better and better as [the season] goes on, and we're showing really early signs of being quite a good team actually.
"Then the final bit is connecting them, because of the age range and the experience range. We have some that have played in the Premier League, to some that actually this is their fourth game in PL2.
"What they expect, what they demand of each other is really different. So at the moment, those connections are developing. They're getting better, but there's still a long way to go."

items.summaryEn: We suffered our first defeat of the Premier League 2 season on Saturday
bodyEn: Our under-21s unbeaten start to the Premier League 2 season came to an end with a 4-1 defeat to Chelsea at Mangata Developments Stadium.
The visitors opened the scoring after 14 minutes through Leo Black, before Reggie Watson found the bottom corner from the penalty spot right on half-time.
Despite a well-taken strike from James Scanlon, second half strikes from Watson and Chizaram Ezenwata secured the victory for the Blues.
FIRST HALF

We created the first chance of the game when Max Dowman threaded a neat through ball into James Scanlon, who saw his effort spilled by Freddy Bernal. Andre Harriman-Annous almost converted the rebound but had the ball swiped from his feet by Bernal.
The Blues then went down the other end of broke the deadlock when Black picked up a loose ball in the penalty area and fired into the corner.
Our young Gunners responded well to going behind and almost had an immediate equaliser when Scanlon's low cross found Harriman-Annous, but the striker's effort was beaten away by Bernal.

After a strong spell for us, the visitors had a great opportunity to net their second ten minutes before the break, but Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli put his effort straight at Jack Porter from eight yards out.
Porter was called into action once again right on half-time, making a stunning reaction save to stop a deflected cross ending up in the bottom corner.
The Blues found their second before half-time though as Watson converted a penalty after Nicoll-Jazuli had been brought down.
SECOND HALF

Chelsea continued to fly forward after the break and had a chance for a third, only for Porter to make another excellent save to deny Nicoll-Jazuli four minutes in the second half. The Blues then somehow didn't convert from the following corner as Justin Osagie missed the target from three yards out.
We sprung a quick counter attack a few minutes later which culminated in Igor Tyjon floating a dangerous cross to the far post, but Harriman-Annous couldn't keep his header down.
Moments later, Harriman-Annous turned provider, picking out Scanlon at the back post, but the winger's header was blocked on the goal line to deny us a route back into the game.
Chelsea got their third from a direct free-kick with 20 minutes to play, Watson finding the corner via the post with a well-taken strike.
We got ourselves on the scoresheet thanks to a fine finish from Scanlon just inside the box, but Ezenwata restored the Blues' three-goal lead in stoppage time.
WHAT IT MEANS
Defeat in north London leaves us with two points from our first three Premier League 2 games.
WHAT'S NEXT
David Horseman's side head to Birmingham City on Friday, September 18. Kick-off is scheduled for 1pm (UK).

items.titleEn: Smith proud of killer instinct in win over Palace
items.summaryEn: Josh Smith praised our attitude to finish off the Eagles on Saturday
bodyEn: Josh Smith was pleased to see our under-18s use the lessons they've learned in the early stages of the season to finish off our win over Crystal Palace on Saturday.
We took a 1-0 lead for the third game in a row (fourth including our UEFA Youth League win over Napoli), but this was the first of those matches in which we've scored the next goal.
"It was a really controlled performance compared to last week," Smith said, "very similar in terms of going 1-0 up.
"The biggest learning from last week was if we get the second goal, then we can have more control with that.

"I didn't like how we started, it was a little bit slow, it took us around half an hour to get going. But as soon as we scored that first goal, the last 15 minutes [of the first half] and the second half, in terms of the territory that we had, was much, much better."
Our performance was a mature one against the Eagles, staying calm throughout and controlling the game.
Smith was especially proud of this element of the performance given the young make-up of the team.
"The best way to sum it up would be a mature performance from a very young team. Once everyone calmed down [after the first goal], there was a lot more control.
"Today we only started with four second years, so very, very pleasing."

Saturday's win was the third game in seven days for several of our young Gunners, with our first UEFA Youth League game against Napoli on Wednesday splitting U18 Premier League games against Southampton and Crystal Palace.
Smith was impressed not only with the fact that we've won all three games, but also the way our young Gunners have managed the significant demands of our schedule.

"There were a lot of boys that travelled to Napoli. This is what we're trying to prepare them for if they do want to have those long-term careers, having to go Tuesday, Saturday, Wednesday, and repeating.

"We have an under-17s game on Tuesday against West Brom, where a lot of the lads will then go again. You can feel the energy shifting, there's a lot more momentum, there's a lot more togetherness within the group."

items.summaryEn: Emerson Nwaneri and Callan Hamill found the net to make it back-to-back wins
bodyEn: Our under-18s secured a second-straight win in the U18 Premier League South with a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace on Saturday afternoon.
Emerson Nwaneri opened the scoring in the first half, latching onto Jayden Maghoma's pinpoint delivery to break the deadlock.
Palace pushed for an equaliser after the break, but a brilliant late strike from Callan Hamill put the game beyond the Eagles' reach and ensured we took all three points.
FIRST HALF
After a slow start to the game, the visitors had the first opportunity when Raihaan Anderson forced an excellent close-range save from Remi Lupinski.
With the Palace chance acting as a wake-up call for our young Gunners, we sprung into action, and almost took the lead when Maghoma's low effort was saved by Lucca Benetton.
The breakthrough came just after the half hour mark with Maghoma picking the ball up on the left wing and picking out Nwaneri, who found the bottom corner from close range.
We could've doubled our lead before the break when Maalik Hashi played a neat one-two with Hamill, only to place his effort wide of the far post.
SECOND HALF
We kept the momentum up at the start of the second half, keeping the Eagles boxed in.
Our best chance in the opening 15 minutes of the half came when Hashi and Nwaneri combined to set up Luiz Munoz on the edge of the box, but the 14-year-old placed his effort just wide.
After changes from both sides, we enjoyed a sustained spell of possession with few chances for either side.
But when Palace stepped up the tempo in the final 15 minutes, we were ready to pounce, and doubled our lead when Hamill rifled a fine effort into the top corner from the edge of the penalty area.
WHAT IT MEANS
Victory moves us up into the top half of the U18 Premier League South table, sitting eighth with seven points from our opening five games.
WHAT'S NEXT
Our under-18s head to East Anglia to take on Norwich City next Saturday, September 19, with kick-off set for 12pm (UK).

items.titleEn: Preview: Arsenal Women v Crystal Palace
items.summaryEn: Women’s Super League football returns to Emirates Stadium for the first time in 2026/27 as we host Crystal Palace at 2.45pm on Sunday, September 13 in N5.
bodyEn: Women’s Super League football returns to Emirates Stadium for the first time in 2026/27 as we host Crystal Palace at 2.45pm on Sunday, September 13 in N5.
We began the season with a 1-0 opening day win away to Brighton & Hove Albion last weekend, while newly-promoted Palace beat Everton 1-0 at home.
Ahead of our clash with the Eagles, find out all you need to know about the opposition below, catch up on the manager’s pre-match quotes, get the latest team news and more.
EAGLES FLYING HIGH
Palace fans couldn’t have asked for much more than a win and a clean sheet in their return to the WSL last Sunday. That came by way of Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s 34th-minute strike against the Toffees.

Jo Potter’s side were promoted to the division after finishing second in the WSL 2 last season. They beat Oxford United in pre-season before losing to Real Madrid and ourselves in August, with Lisa Baum and Chloe Kelly on the scoresheet for us.

As for recruitment, Palace have made six permanent signings, nameely Sierra Enge, Bethany England, Lexi Lloyd-Smith, Shannon O’Brien, Molly Bartrip and Shanade Hopcroft, bringing in a wealth of experience, while also recruiting former Gunner Teyah Golder as well as Fuka Tsunoda on loan.

One quirk to last weekend’s match was that Palace illegally used four substitution windows against Everton (clubs are only allowed to use three). The team of refereeing officials have been stood down for the second round of fixtures, while the investigation continues.
RENÉE'S PREVIEW

Slegers: “We know what we want to create for ourselves there, and that's us on that pitch, in that setting, together with the fans and bring the fans with us, and that's always a really lovely and nice atmosphere that we create, like all the moments that we've had there so far with the supporters.

“So I really look forward to creating that again on Sunday. So I can only speak for myself and what we can create for ourselves and how that fuels us and our performances.” - Read every word of Renée’s pre-Crystal Palace press conference.
TEAM NEWS

There are now fresh team news concerns following last weekend's win over Brighton, with the same players remaining unavailable (Michelle Agyemang, Katie Reid and Daphne van Domselaar). New signing Élisa de Almeida is now available to be selected.
FACTS AND STATS

We have won each of our last four meetings with Crystal Palace in all competitions by an aggregate score of 20-0, winning 5-0 at home and 4-0 away in our only previous WSL campaign together in 2024/25.

We are unbeaten in each of our last 19 home games in the WSL (W16 D3), already a club record; overall, we are 18 games unbeaten (W14 D4) and only once have had a longer run, going 19 undefeated between August 2011 and October 2012.

In 2026, we have kept nine WSL clean sheets in 12 games – four more than any other team. Of teams to play more than one game in a year in the WSL, only Chelsea in 2017 (10 clean sheets in 13 games, 77%) have a better clean sheet ratio in a year than us this year (75%). We’ve faced just 1.5 shots on target per game (18 in 12 games), the lowest ratio by a team in a calendar year in WSL history.

We have trailed for just 8% of our WSL games in the last two seasons, the lowest ratio of any side. In our last 15 matches, we’ve trailed for just 21 minutes and 42 seconds, all in the same game against Brighton in May 2026, a 1-1 draw.

Georgia Stanway completed 98 passes on her WSL debut for us on MD1, the most ever by a Gunners player on their first WSL appearance. In WSL history, only Abby Dahlkemper has completed more on her debut for a specific club (111 for Manchester City in January 2021).
Steph Catley could make her 100th WSL appearance in this game, becoming the second Australian player to hit that landmark after her current teammate Caitlin Foord (119).
REF WATCH

Declan Brown has been appointed to be the man in the middle for Sunday’s fixture. He has seen over three matches so far this season in League One, League Two and the Carabao Cup, handing out nine yellow cards in the process.

bodyEn: Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.

The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.

Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.

This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

items.summaryEn: Get the latest team news, stats, tactics, a guide to the Black Cats' start, live coverage and more in our essential guide to the game
bodyEn: After recording five wins from five to kick off the campaign, we look to keep our 100% record intact when we head all the way to the Stadium of Light for a clash with Sunderland on Saturday night (8pm UK).

Wednesday’s hard-fought victory in a scorching Naples was the first of four away games in succession successfully navigated, and now we’ll hope our fine record on the road continues, as domestically we have lost just one of our last 12 league away games, winning each of the last three.

Regis Le Bris’ team did hold us to a draw in this fixture last season, when their achievements earned them the opportunity to face some of Europe’s biggest teams, and while Black Cats fans will be relishing that prospect, a visit from the champions under the weekend lights will also be a tantalising test to see if they’ll be able to replicate recent achievements.
EUROPE ON HORIZON

After a stunning top-flight return saw the Black Cats finish seventh to secure a Europa League spot - the first time they’d ever reached Europe via their league placing - Le Fee stuck with the majority of his squad, but brought in five summer signings, most notably Belgium’s experienced right-back Thomas Meunier and Ecuadorian striker Nilson Angulo.

He scored in a 2-1 defeat at Ipswich Town on the opening day after a 90th-minute concession, but Sunderland bounced back by maintaining their strong home form with a 1-0 victory over Fulham, with Wilson Isidor on target. Last weekend saw an Enzo Le Fee penalty salvage a 1-1 draw at Brentford, and the win, loss and draw leaves them 12th in the division.

Another home victory, this time a 1-0 success over Hull City, saw them progress to the fourth round of the Carabao Cup on Tuesday, and after our game has taken place, they’ll welcome AZ Alkmaar to the Stadium of Light for its first-ever taste of continental action.
WHAT THE MANAGERS SAY

Arteta: “We experienced last season how tough it’s going to be. It’s an unbelievable atmosphere, and it’s great to play in these kinds of games. We know how ready they’re going to be. We know the importance of it and we’ll be ready to be on that pitch. We’ll compete like we always do, we’ll try to be better than the opponent and win the game.

“Last year, we dropped points there, especially in the last minutes. We experienced and learned a lot from that game for the previous one. Tomorrow, again, we'll discuss many things that we need to be aware of and where we want to take the game, what their qualities are and how we’ll try to nullify them.”

Le Bris: “To be competitive in this kind of game, we have to be ourselves. Our underdog mentality, togetherness and connection with the fans is crucial. We have to have clarity in our game model, because they have so much flexibility.

“We have to make it as uncomfortable and as difficult as possible. The supporters are a powerful driver, but it starts from us. When we are proactive, they are behind us and they feed the energy for the press and the second ball.”
TEAM NEWS

Jurrien Timber is back in training after missing the summer and season so far with a groin injury, while Cristhian Mosquera is also edging closer to a comeback after sitting out the wins against Chelsea and Napoli over the past week.
William Saliba remains our only other injury issue, but he is out long-term as he deals with a back issue.
As for our opponents, Le Bris has confirmed that Romaine Mundle and Habib Diarra are Sunderland’s only injury absentees.
The former has a knee injury that will keep him out until Christmas, while the Senegalese international midfielder has a hamstring problem and will miss another month.
TALKING TACTICS

Adrian Clarke: Sunderland will line up in a 4-2-3-1 with playmaker Le Fee playing behind striker Brian Brobbey. Last season, the muscular Dutchman was a handful inside the box, and the Wearsiders caused us issues with direct football. As it proved effective, there is no reason to suggest that the home side won’t go long again.

The Black Cats are one of the best pressing sides in the division, so we must ready ourselves for a physical, full-blooded contest. Good at unsettling opponents with their tenacity and work rate, Le Bris’ side are an awkward outfit to find your flow against, and have faced just five shots on target so far, the fewest of all Premier League sides.

Out wide, our opponents also have good quality. Left winger Nilson Angulo is a tricky operator with a penchant for flair, while the other side, full-backs-turned-wingers Trai Hume or Thomas Meunier will provide great energy. Le Bris will ask plenty of Granit Xhaka, as his 23 ball recoveries since the start of the campaign ranks him second in the division.

Sunderland only lost four of 19 home games in 2025/26 and have kicked off this season with a couple of 1-0 victories in all competitions. The longer they stay in the match, the more intimidating the atmosphere will be.
FACTS AND STATS
Sunderland have won just one of their last 29 Premier League meetings with us (D10 L18), and are winless in 17 since a 1-0 victory in November 2009.
We are looking to start a league campaign by winning our first two away games for a fourth time in the last five seasons.

We haven’t lost any of our last 23 evening kick-offs in the Premier League since a home loss to West Ham United in December 2024. On the road meanwhile, we are unbeaten in 11 evening kick-offs, since being defeated by Manchester City in April 2023.
We have gone 1-0 up in eight of our last nine away Premier League games. When scoring first, we are unbeaten in our last 31 away league matches since a 2-1 loss at Fulham in December 2023.
Sunderland meanwhile have won just two of their eight evening kick-offs in the Premier League last season.
The Black Cats have won their last two Premier League home games, and last won three in a row at the Stadium of Light in January/February 2012.
Sunderland haven’t won a Premier League game in September at the Stadium of Light since 2012, going winless in eight since.
We have the lowest xG against of any side in the Premier League (0.93), while only Sunderland (5) have faced fewer shots on target than us (6).

Kai Havertz has covered more distance than any other striker in the Premier League (32.9 km), while only Fulham’s Gonzalo Garcia (52) has made more sprints among strikers than the German this term (50).
Only Morgan Rogers (9) has created more chances in open play than Christos Tzolis (8) in the Premier League this season.
MATCH OFFICIALS

John Brooks has been handed control of this fixture, with his last Arsenal appointment coming in February when we drew 1-1 at Brentford. We had won the previous three games he had refereed before that, including victories over West Ham and Brighton last term, but we have only triumphed in half of the eight matches he’s presided over.

Sunderland meanwhile have won four out of six the Melton Mowbray-based official has managed, including a pair of wins against Everton last season. Brooks has been quite card-happy in 26/27, dishing out 25 yellows in four games in all competitions, including at least five per match.
Referee: John BrooksAssistants: James Mainwaring, Wade SmithFourth official: Elliot BellVAR: Stuart AttwellAssistant VAR: Edward Smart
PREVIOUS WEARSIDE TRIPS

We have lost just one of our last 14 visits to the Stadium of Light in the Premier League, with that defeat coming in November 2009. However, a late Brian Brobbey goal saw us depart with just a point last season after a 2-2 draw, with Dan Ballard’s opener cancelled out by Bukayo Saka and Leandro Trossard strikes.

Our previous visit came in October 2016, when we ran out 4-1 victors, with braces from Alexis Sanchez and Olivier Giroud, to cruise past David Moyes’ side, while six months earlier, we played out a goalless draw at the same venue.
LIVE COVERAGE

There will be live commentary of the game on Arsenal.com and The Arsenal app (download now on iOS/Android) from just before kick-off, when Dan Roebuck and Adrian Clarke will be behind the mics guiding you through all the on-field action.
You can also find out which broadcasters are showing the action live, wherever you are in the world.

bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.

Arsenal’s flight to Italy on Tuesday for their Champions League opener against Napoli was delayed for more than five hours, with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time.
The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe, thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner.

Arteta has a reputation for his innovative methods having previously employed pickpockets during pre-season training camps and preparing for a trip to Anfield by pumping crowd noises through a speaker.

The Arsenal manager has now explained how his players have been trained to expect things to go wrong. “I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season,” he said. “So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, get to the stadium very late, change the routine as soon as the players have to do something else.
“Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic, and I don’t want the players, the staff as well, panicking.

“So, when that happens, adapt to it. ‘OK, we have another two or three hours on the plane, how can we use them?’ Play together, spend some time together, sleep, use it, but ­certainly don’t complain and then use it as an excuse because that’s not helpful at all.”

Asked what other methods he has employed, Arteta added: “Just delay the meals, delay the transport, take a different route. We have done many things: make the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less [massage] beds. Those kind of things. Because we are going to have to adapt to different contexts and we will try to anticipate it and create the best possible conditions. But when there is that element of stress or ­surprise on matchday, it’s important [to be prepared].”

Arsenal travel to Sunderland on Saturday night looking to extend their 100% start to the new campaign after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last year. Leandro Trossard scored Arsenal’s second goal before Brian Brobbey’s late equaliser and Arteta contrasted the Belgium forward’s reaction to leaving in the summer with that of Gabriel Jesus, whohas complained that he was kept in the dark over his future before being sold to Barcelona. “No one told me nothing,” said the Brazilian, who was made to train separately from the rest of Arsenal’s squad before moving to Barcelona. Trossard, meanwhile, was at the Emirates for last week’s win over Chelsea having joined Beskitas in July.

“Very surprised, to be fair, especially because with Gabriel I had an individual talk in the dressing room,” said Arteta. “And the words that we used for each other, it was all about gratitude. So, I don’t know. It’s OK. Sometimes I understand when you have to deliver bad news or news that people don’t expect. Those things are reactive. Somebody has to be the bad cop; if I have to be, I have to be.

“What is important is normally what happens three months later, six months later. When Trossard comes in, he’s in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relation you have with all the players that they left, at some point their relationship has been really good. I hope that’s the same case.”

bodyEn: With 10 top-flight goal contributions between them across three games already this season, the Chelsea trio of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer are the early pace-setters for the Premier League’s most prolific, fluid and high-octane attacking unit. But on the occasion of his 100th Premier League appearance, a scruffier and more ungainly unit will be hoping to steal their thunder, as high-flying Hull try to register a top-flight win against Chelsea for the very first time. Yet to score this season but with a couple of near misses to his name, what Oli McBurnie has thus far lacked in goal contributions he has more than made up for with selfless graft and off-the-ball grunt work, making a total mockery of Steve Clarke’s decision not to include him in Scotland’s World Cup squad. The Hull striker ought to prove a real handful for a decidedly porous home defence, and a goal would be a fitting way to mark a century of Premier League appearances. Chelsea have not won any of their past four league matches against promoted opposition and, given Hull’s blistering start to the season, victory on Saturday seems anything but a foregone conclusion. Barry Glendenning
Chelsea v Hull, Saturday 3pm (all times BST)

This might be an opportune moment for Álvaro Arbeloa to meet Andoni Iraola, though perhaps not his Liverpool team. With three defeats and seven goals conceded from his first three Premier League games as Fulham head coach, questions are already being asked over the former Liverpool defender’s ambitious approach. Just as they were when Iraola failed to win any of his first nine league games in charge of Bournemouth. Trust yourself and the process, might be the Liverpool head coach’s advice if asked. Fulham have been creative under Arbeloa but are easily exposed defensively. Liverpool, starting to click in attack under their new head coach, have the assets to exploit Fulham’s weaknesses and subject Arbeloa to an uncomfortable Anfield return. Iraola’s wide options could be reduced, however, with Bradley Barcola suffering cramp on Wednesday – his first start since France’s World Cup semi-final loss – and Cody Gakpo nursing a minor injury. Andy Hunter
Liverpool v Fulham, Saturday 3pm

Cheick Doucouré has had a rotten run of luck with injuries. Just when the Mali midfielder looked as if he was ready to make a first Crystal Palace appearance since January 2025 in Tuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Middlesbrough, he was taken ill. Pierre Sage revealed last week that Doucouré looked as if he had “given him one million dollars” when he was informed he would be part of the matchday squad at Fulham, where Palace got off the mark with a 3-2 victory. Sage has confirmed that the 26-year-old, who has been sidelined with two serious knee injuries but was once a transfer target for Liverpool, could be involved against Ipswich at Selhurst Park on Saturday. Whenever he does return it is sure to be a heartwarming moment. Ed Aarons
Crystal Palace v Ipswich, Saturday 3pm

The midfield battle between Brentford and Bournemouth will be crucial on Saturday, with Vitaly Janelt and Mamadou Sangaré setting the tempo for Keith Andrews’ physical side. Brentford top the Premier League for aerial duels won (22.3 per 90 mins), interceptions (11.3 per 90), and fouls committed (16.3 per 90). “They defend well as a team, their high pressing is good,” said Bournemouth’s Marco Rose, who is hoping to guide his side to a first Premier League victory of the season. “Their transition, they have fast players. They have quality everywhere on the pitch, and every situation.” Rose’s answer for Brentford’s aggressiveness should be Alex Scott, who leads his team for interceptions and has drawn nine fouls so far this campaign – the fourth-highest tally in the league. Late drama could also be the deciding factor at the Vitality Stadium. Despite leading in all three of their opening league fixtures, Bournemouth have picked up just two points and four of their five goals conceded have arrived from the 84th minute onwards. History favours their opponents too, as the Cherries have failed to win any of their eight top-flight meetings with the Bees. Yara El-Shaboury
Bournemouth v Brentford, Saturday 3pm

A summer of change at Aston Villa inevitably prompted plenty of noise but most of their new signings were long-standing targets, none more so than Nicolas Jackson. Unai Emery kickstarted Jackson’s career at Villarreal and, after reuniting at Villa, the Senegal striker scored his first goal at Club Brugge on Tuesday after his initial £47.5m move. Jackson has replaced Ollie Watkins, who proved a reliable source of goals across six straight top-flight seasons, and the early evidence has been encouraging. “I had a couple of fights with him when he was at Chelsea so when he first came in I thought: ‘What’s he going to be like?’ but he’s a brilliant guy,” said the Villa captain, John McGinn. “There’s a lot of expectation with the transfer fee but he’s going to be a huge player for us.” Ben Fisher
Aston Villa v Nottingham Forest, Saturday 3pm

Only the most pessimistic home fans at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium will be gripped by anything resembling the kind of dread, anxiety and outright terror that accompanied Everton’s visit on the final day of last season, but the return of David Moyes’ side so early in the current campaign will still make for nervous viewing. With no goals and just one point on the board after three league games, fan faith in Roberto De Zerbi – and the hundreds of millions of pounds lavished upon new signings – has created a prevailing presumption that Tottenham will soon start firing on at least some, if not all, cylinders. In Everton, Spurs welcome a team whose record in this corner of north London is worse than any other top-flight side’s. Should they fail to beat a team who have taken just seven points from the past 51 available to them away at Tottenham, the sounds of early but outright mutiny are likely to be audible from the stands. BG
Tottenham v Everton, Saturday 5.30pm

Old acquaintance will be renewed at the Stadium of Light on Saturday evening. While Sunderland’s captain and midfield anchor, Granit Xhaka, needs no introduction to his former north London public, the home centre-half Dan Ballard is a former Arsenal youth captain who joined the Gunners’ academy at the age of eight. Then there is Bruno Guimarães. Newcastle’s former captain can expect a hot reception as his new side aim to extend their season-opening run of five straight wins (including the Community Shield). “Arsenal are flying, they’re one of the best teams in Europe,” says Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager. “It will be challenging but I’m very excited to experience this situation again.” Thanks to goals from Ballard and Brian Brobbey, Le Bris choreographed a 2-2 Premier League draw against Mikel Arteta’s side on Wearside last November. “When you face a strong opponent you can become a bit shy but the most important thing is to be ourselves,” says Le Bris. “Arsenal are so adaptive they will find solutions, so we must be flexible.” Louise Taylor
Sunderland v Arsenal, Saturday 8pm

One of three teams, along with Aston Villa and Tottenham, yet to score a top-flight goal this season, Coventry were extremely unfortunate not to break their duck at Manchester City last weekend. Their having narrowly avoided handing Frank Lampard’s side an early opener, it took a string of excellent saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma to ensure City took three points at the death. “They played really well against Manchester City and created a lot of chances,” said Fabian Hürzeler, who takes his Brighton team to the CBS Arena on Sunday afternoon. Having been scathing in his criticism of his own side’s lack of energy and intensity in their woeful first-half performance against Leeds, the German will be aware that a similarly lethargic performance from his team is unlikely to go unpunished. Particularly away from home against a promoted team that may be firing blanks, but visibly grew in confidence with each passing minute of their defeat by one of the league’s best teams. BG
Coventry v Brighton, Sunday 2pm

Manchester derby No 199 features a fascinating showdown between two young managers operating in the sport’s rarefied air: Michael Carrick, 45, who seeks to guide Manchester United to an 82nd victory in the fixture, and Enzo Maresca, 46, who aims for Manchester City’s 63rd. As the great Pep Guardiola’s successor, the visiting Italian can be delighted at his team’s perfect record from their four games under him since the Community Shield defeat. Carrick, though, should be disappointed at the return from an opening three matches as United’s permanent manager: a defeat at Hull and draw at Everton, with the 5-2 home win over Ipswich sandwiched between. United fans will protest beforehand about the club’s approach to eradicating ticket touting, and the occasion should be particularly spicy and vibrant. Jamie Jackson
Manchester United v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm

Two teams unbeaten in the Premier League this season, two German managers in the dugouts and a Monday night goalkeeping beauty contest at Elland Road. While Daniel Farke welcomes his compatriot Matthias Jaissle to West Yorkshire for the first time, James Trafford – the £40m England keeper Newcastle tried to sign on three separate occasions – will be in goal for Leeds. The visitors eventually turned their attentions to the £26m Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who arrived on Tyneside from Braga in July. So far at least, Jaissle is delighted by the 24-year-old’s performances. “Lukas is an amazing signing,” said Jaissle. “Coming to the Premier League and dealing with the pressure is not easy and, as a keeper, that pressure is something else. I like Lukas a lot. He’s so calm but so mature as well. There’s not even a hint of nervousness. He gives the whole team confidence. That helps a lot.” LT
Leeds v Newcastle, Monday 8pm

bodyEn: During Covid, when sport was back but behind closed doors, I hosted a number of strange online shows to fill the void of real life. The highlight was chatting to Darren Gough about a lifesize bronze rhinoceros for 45 minutes to 15 small boxes on a Zoom call. I don’t recall who it was for and where the rhinoceros came from – but it might be in his garden.

I ended up doing virtual pre-match corporate Zoom calls for Heineken before Europa League games. It was the wifi version of Club Wembley: a Q&A happening on stage between a generic host and some random ex-pro while you’re trying to chat to your mate and eat an unidentified square of meat with some dauphinoise potatoes.

I’d be in my little square talking to Luis García in his little square about the ghost goal while an assorted group of faces and living rooms or kitchen tables would stare at you, perhaps interested, perhaps not. Did they even want to be there? Were we on mute while someone from marketing was filling a spare box on my laptop watching Death In Paradise on the TV behind me?

Certainly it was hard to create an amazing vibe with Mark van Bommel while his internet connection crashed and a little note on a Google doc appeared telling me to fill for 25 minutes with my favourite memories of the Europa League. Did these disembodied heads in front of me want the deep dive they got on Tony Parks’ heroics in 1984? How many of them knew about Gary Mabbutt playing centre mid and marking Enzo Scifo out of the game?

One of the guests was Dimitar Berbatov. You’d log on half an hour before the show and say hello, try to build some kind of electric rapport with a man in Bulgaria (I think) presumably looking to get in and get out and get back on with whatever social distancing life in Sofia had to offer.

He may have not had Akabusi levels of energy, and his economy of language was not unlike his playing style – why use a hundred words when one will do? But he was into it and did the job perfectly. I absolutely loved Berbatov as a player. Watching him pluck a goalkick out of the sky was more beautiful than watching a lot of other players banging one in from 25 yards. There’s a YouTube video called Dimitar Berbatov – the most underrated first touch ever? It begins with him standing like a lamp-post on the halfway line at Craven Cottage and stopping a crossfield ball stone dead like it’s an anvil.

Back to the Zoom call: I welcome Dimitar, he says hello, I explain my admiration for him, and then say to him that he made football look easy. Did he find it easy? “Yes” he replied. Totally matter of fact. Not trying to impress – just explaining that football was easy.

And for someone like Berbatov, it is a different level to “good touch for a big man”. This is the ultimate type of grace on a football pitch. And perhaps it is reserved for tall, skilful players. I’ve probably used the word languid already but I can’t think of any other use of the word – reserved for players who are almost balletic.

Is it insane to say it’s more aesthetically pleasing than seeing a Messi or a Maradona waltz through a defence? It almost feels as if a low centre of gravity gives you an unfair advantage when it comes to technical skill. No flailing arms and legs to get in the way of you being naturally brilliant.

My biased brain instantly goes to Glenn Hoddle walking through the Oxford United defence with one sway, sitting the keeper down with a movement of the leg. It’s all saying: “This is easier for me than it is for you.”

Which brings us to Kai Havertz – and that dummy against Chelsea. The more and more football becomes that David Mitchell sketch, the more surprised I am that there are still moments in a game that lead to some involuntary noise from deep within.

The ball from Christos Tzolis is definitely for him. Havertz points in front to where he wants the ball. If it’s played there he can probably get a shot away first time. But when it comes, controlling the ball would have been a sensible choice. Back to goal. He could have turned and shot, or just kept the ball. There are lots of good players to pass it to.

Even the way he lifts his left leg at the last second to let the ball run through to Martin Ødegaard is delightful. It’s easy to forget the pace of the game at this level. And when you’re watching on TV where it’s much easier to see the pass you also forget these guys don’t have that view.

Someone somewhere will have done a report on Havertz’s scanning abilities. He doesn’t appear to look behind to check where Ødegaard is. But awareness is hard to calculate. He just knows. And he does it all in a split second, not even. How wonderful that you can do so much without even touching the ball.

A lot of people do quite well out of repeatedly asking whether Arsenal need a centre-forward, so I don’t want to do them out of work. And Havertz isn’t perfect – he isn’t Robbie Fowler in the box. But he has scored in two Champions League finals. He did win the league last season. A lot of beautiful graceful players tend to be beautiful and graceful without delivering on the biggest occasions. Havertz does both. And when he gets it right, it looks easy to him. Imagine finding it easy.

bodyEn: Declan Rice has insisted his body can sustain more than 60 appearances again this season, despite Arsenal’s concerns after he played through pain at the World Cup.

Rice racked up 69 appearances last season for Arsenal and England but revealed during the World Cup he had been managing neural back and hamstring pain, for which he is understood to have received a pain-killing injection, after a hamstring injury in December. It is understood Arsenal are monitoring the 27-year-old’s workload closely after he had only three weeks off before returning to training a week before the Community Shield last month.

Rice came off the bench to replace Bruno Guimarães in the victory over Manchester City in Cardiff and has since started all Arsenal’s matches, with Guimarães’ return from an injury being managed. A major reason why Arsenal bought the Brazil midfielder for £75m from Newcastle was to take some strain off from Rice, although it was noticeable that Rice played all of Wednesday’s Champions League victory at Napoli, with Mikel Merino coming off for Guimarães.

“I think for the last six seasons, even since my West Ham days when they were in Europe, I’ve played 60-plus every season,” Rice said. “So I think it is sustainable because I’ve shown that I can do it.

“It’s just about maintaining it, maintaining the level and the consistency of the performances. For me, that’s the main thing, showing up every week, giving a good account of myself and helping the team win. I’ve been lucky enough to be able to do that. So I’m really hungry to be able to do that again this season.”

It is understood Arsenal offered Rice more time off after the World Cup exploits but that he was keen to return for the start of the season. He is expected to be part of Thomas Tuchel’s squad for Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia when it is announced next Friday, although whether he features in all four matches remains to be seen, with Arsenal likely to request that he and Bukayo Saka are given another opportunity to rest. Rice said he had found things “tough” during the World Cup but is adamant he is feeling “refreshed”.

“I feel really good at the minute, in really good form, so we’ll make it continue,” he said. “I think everyone knew I had an issue with a neural hamstring. But also on the top of the Premier League season, which was so demanding, the Champions League, to then play a World Cup in that heat really does take its toll. I’m a player that goes on the pitch, wants to be fresh and give 100% every time I put on an England shirt. Yes, there were stages where I felt really, really good and stages where I didn’t feel so good. There were a few things that frustrated me, just with myself, just not feeling 100%. It’s one of those things I just had to manage.”

Rice is one of three England players nominated for the Ballon d’Or this week, with Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane. The ceremony, traditionally in Paris, will take place in London on 26 October as a tribute to Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the inaugural award in 1956, and Rice has backed Kane to become the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001. “I would Iove to see Harry win it,” he said. “So I’m wishing him all the best in that.”

bodyEn: Valdas Dambrauskas can reel off the questions and answers without a moment’s pause. Who won the first Academy Award for best actor in 1929? It was Emil Jannings, even if someone else might have been tempted to go with Charlie Chaplin. Which country publishes the highest number of daily newspapers? India was the clear winner. Can you name the nation that produces the most electricity per capita in the world? His family, watching back home, clasped heads in hands but he was right: back then, in 2002, the answer was his native Lithuania.

It was enough to win Dambrauskas about £725 in his appearance on Six Zeros – A Million, the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? “At that time it was quite big money,” he says. “I could have bought a flat in my home town; it was a very difficult period there and they were almost free. But my plan was to go to England and follow my dream to become a coach, and that’s how it started.”

More than two and a half decades later the story continues at Old Trafford where Dambrauskas will manage the Azerbaijani champions, Sabah, in their Champions League debut on Thursday night. The club’s journey is some tale in itself given Sabah, who came through a dramatic playoff with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, did not exist until 2017. But the path taken by their head coach, a 25-year-old office worker with only a modest football background when his general knowledge skills were put on display, is virtually unparalleled in the modern game.

The money he won helped Dambrauskas and his girlfriend, now wife, to move to north London and establish themselves in an alien environment. “I would have done it anyway – the show came in the middle of our planning,” he says of the move, which became an ambition after a work visit to Norway in 2000.

In Scandinavia he had grasped the extent of the Premier League’s incipient popularity. “I realised this was where real football is. There was no pathway to coaching in Lithuania if you hadn’t been a player; it was impossible. But if I could take a course in England, maybe I could get a chance to step on the ladder at home.”

Dambrauskas spent eight years in London. “The start was very, very difficult. I wasn’t speaking decent English, had no contacts, we didn’t know anyone, we lived in different places, did all kinds of jobs.” He worked in a Muswell Hill pub, delivered newspapers in the area, held down jobs in a nursery school, as a gardener, in sales, and as a self-employed handyman, often simultaneously. The hours were relentless but so was the young man’s focus.

It was a life of an immigrant couple straining every sinew to make their way. Their first child was born in 2004; by then Dambrauskas, who had studied philosophy and social sciences in Lithuania, had enrolled on a sports science and coaching course at London Metropolitan University. From his classroom on the 10th floor he could see the Emirates Stadium sprouting up during that spell of Arsenal invincibility.

The Access to Sports Project, based in Finsbury Park, is a stone’s throw from Arsenal but galaxies away in another sense. It is where Dambrauskas landed his first coaching role, giving sessions to children on Saturday mornings and during school holidays. His next step is all the more remarkable for what has passed since. A round of interviews with Manchester United Soccer Schools brought the chance to work with youngsters around the country, and sometimes on residential trips abroad, under the banner of the then serial title winners. Despite the name it was a far cry from even academy football, but the injection of confidence was transformative.

“It was John Shiels, CEO of the Manchester United Foundation, who gave me the chance. I don’t know what he saw in me – I came in with very broken English and couldn’t express myself as I can now – but he really supported me. At the end of the year he wrote me an appraisal of what I’d done. He said that I was good and could do much more. It was a massive, massive boost for me.”

Through a friend at university, Dambrauskas became involved with the community sports organisation London Tigers. “He told me they always needed coaches.” Eventually he took charge of their semi-professional team, which played in the Spartan South Midlands League. “That was where it really started, coaching at some kind of level.” It meant managing in the FA Vase and the early rounds of the FA Cup.

Dambrauskas also undertook part-time roles at Fulham and Brentford before working as a sports activator for Central YMCA on Tottenham Court Road. He would later take a broader role as sports development manager at London Tigers and took his coaching badges at the London Football Association. “It was a time with no holidays, no days off. I’m a big reader, I read all the time and studied constantly. Sometimes I would finish my university work on the bus. I took every kind of education I could and went to every possible course for every meeting.

“Over the years I had countless interviews for coaching roles, for jobs at centres of excellency in London and outside, so many CVs and applications, but I understood early on that it’s very difficult in England to get on the ladder and that to coach at professional level there was probably impossible. If there is a story where someone is starting in the community scheme and going all the way to become a head coach, I am still to find it.”

By late 2010 he felt ready to pursue what had originally been the end goal: a role in Lithuania. He had started working with their under-17s and agreed to join Ekranas, national champions at the time, as assistant manager. “I had the London Tigers job, 15 hours a week at Brentford and some other things here and there. We had a good life and people thought I was crazy going back home and earning about a fifth of what I was getting in England. But the biggest risk in life is not to take risks.

“I’m forever grateful to my wife for being behind me. We always faced questions: twenty- or thirtysomething guy always studying, trying to work in football, spending all his money on books and courses rather than buying an apartment or something for the family. But I’m very happy with how it turned out and nobody questions those decisions now.”

A kaleidoscopic career bloomed. By December 2014 he had become head coach at Zalgiris Vilnius, the biggest club in Lithuania, winning two more league titles and various cups in a move that felt unthinkable during a humble upbringing in the tiny northern town Pakruojis. “My childhood was not a gift. My dad died when I was 11, and if he knew that I had the job at Zalgiris and that we won so many trophies he would be the happiest person in the world.”

Dambrauskas was not content to stop there. “You are basically nobody and suddenly you get this job. Then you have to prove yourself to everybody again and again and again. So you reached this step on the ladder but what’s next? How do you go to the next level?”

After three years he joined the upwardly mobile Latvian club RFS but harboured concerns about the prospects of leaving the small Baltic football bubble. In the event he need not have worried. Since 2020 he has managed in Croatia with Gorica and Hajduk Split – the latter are “like a tattoo you can’t ever take out, it leaves a mark on you” – in Bulgaria with Ludogorets, in Greece with OFI Crete, in Cyprus with Omonia and with the Hungarian club Diosgyor, who he describes as having “one of the biggest hidden football potentials in Europe”.

Itinerant career paths such as that are, especially in eastern and southern Europe, nothing new. But Sabah had been courting Dambrauskas for two years before he took over in 2025. Once the stars had aligned, he worked a miracle. In 2024-25, Sabah had finished 41 points behind the biggest club in Azerbaijan, Qarabag. Last season Sabah beat them to the title by nine points, earning their crack at the Champions League qualifiers. “I’m really grateful to Qarabag. Every game against them is like taking a master’s degree.”

He waxes lyrical about the stability and facilities available at well-backed Sabah, who were cheered on with fervour befitting a national team when they thrillingly overcame an injury-time deficit against Be’er Sheva. Their success has come with a multinational squad that plays bold, front-foot football in the style he preaches. “But if you don’t understand the human being in front of you, it’s very difficult to pass him your ideas and build trust,” he says.

“What is important in east Africa can be completely different from what someone needs in west Africa or anywhere across Europe. You need to be able to understand different cultures, different traditions, different ways of speaking or behaving. Without that it’s impossible to do anything, and I believe this is where my strength lies.”

It is a glorious piece of circularity that Dambrauskas and Sabah will be watched from the stands on Thursday by a number of his old colleagues from Manchester United Soccer Schools. He beams at the thought; none of this could have seemed remotely attainable during their time on the grass together. “But I had this belief. I had this confidence all the time that I could do it.”

He is equally delighted that the draw has also brought a January visit to Arsenal, that huge presence in his eyeline during those years studying on Holloway Road. He is 49 and would surely lever himself among Europe’s most sought-after coaching properties if he can take Sabah further. “We’re going to respect everyone but not be afraid of anyone. There’s a very nice song by the Lithuanian band Colours of Bubbles called Truth or Dare. Very soon we’re going to find out the truth about ourselves and what we can do. It will be very beneficial for us because I don’t want this club to be a one-day wonder.” As final answers go, it may be his most significant yet.

bodyEn: Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League.

The Brazilian was a surprise omission from this week’s 30-strong list of candidates for the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.

The summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.
There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.

“The most important thing is we are playing like a team, like one unit,” the Barcelona head coach, Hansi Flick, said. “We controlled the game, we are dominant and this is fantastic to see. This is our style and how we want to play.”

Ferran Torres scored a hat-trick and Ousmane Dembélé also starred as Paris Saint-Germain began their quest to win a third successive Champions League title by thrashing Slovan Bratislava 6-1 at the Parc des Princes.

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembélé had scored twice by the midway point of the first half in the French capital, and then set up Spain’s World Cup final hero Torres to make it 3-0 by the interval.

Torres, a close-season signing from Barcelona, added two more just after the restart to complete his hat-trick before the hour mark, with Suleiman Camara pulling one back for the Slovakian champions and Fabián Ruiz then sealing PSG’s win.
Elsewhere, Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory over Viking Stavanger.

He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot.

Demirovic quickly re-established the lead ​in the ​26th minute and then completed ​the hat-trick with a hooked volley six minutes later. “For me personally it was the perfect start and also for the team as a whole,” Demirovic told Dazn.

West Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards.

Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.

The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve.

James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. Either Charlton or QPR could have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games.

Norwich moved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitors Birmingham 2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out.

Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season. Press Association
Sporting, quarter-finalists last season for the first time since 1983, fought back to see off Galatasaray 3-1 in Lisbon.

Galatasaray took an early lead through Gonçalo Inacio’s own goal but Geny ​Catamo punished poor defending to equalise in the 27th minute. Luis Suárez converted a 57th-minute penalty to put Sporting ahead and a blistering free kick from Rodrigo Zalazar six minutes later sealed the win.

The England midfielder returned to England this summer, joining us from Bayern Munich to compete in the WSL for the first time since 2022.
Georgia joined Frimmy at the Sobha Realty Training Centre to chat about signing for us, our training camp in La Manga and the story of her "whatever the weather" tattoo.
There was also the usual mix of sing-songs and Frimmy's Target Game, as well as plenty of laughs before Georgia set off for training.
